1993.blurb: Archers of Loaf launched *Icky Mettle* in September 1993 on Alias Records, a Los Angeles independent that had signed them and provided a van — the practical foundation of everything that followed. Out of Chapel Hill, where Superchunk and Polvo were already running the same playbook, they worked the indie circuit hard: the Middle East in Cambridge, Lounge Ax in Chicago three times in nine months, college towns, 300-cap rooms where you either won the room or you didn't. The debut peaked at #18 on CMJ and charted 21 weeks. By 1994 they were in the UK and Sweden before a second album existed, building on word of mouth alone.

quotes.text: We were all broke as a joke and I was subsisting on $.25 Little Debbie snax.
We would show up in far flung towns and there were people who knew some of our music and were happy to see us. It was wonderful.

1995.blurb: *Vee Vee* came out March 6, 1995, recorded in Chicago on a $6,000 budget, and the band was back on the road before the reviews landed. Their highest-profile slot that year came opening for Weezer on the World Domination Tour — an audience mismatch that put an abrasive Chapel Hill four-piece in front of arenas full of people who had not come for them. By fall the original van was gone, replaced by a Ryder truck and a rent-a-car, two vehicles covering the continent while they played most nights. Seventy-three documented shows that year, Troubadour to Bottom of the Hill to Crocodile Cafe, deep into a circuit that wasn't getting smaller.

quotes.text: That was a difficult tour for us. We were chasing a bus tour in our van, and that made the logistics brutal.
quotes.attr: Matt Gentling [on the Weezer tour], *Perfect Sound Forever*, October 2018

quotes.text: We were assured for years that if we stopped touring, we would be forgotten and languish, so we hadn't let up.

1992.blurb: Randall Lee arrived in Chicago from Adelaide — already a veteran of the Cannanes, already peripatetic by disposition — and assembled the first American incarnation of Ashtray Boy around drummer J. Niimi and bassist David Trumfio, who would later produce Wilco. Liz Phair, then still pre-*Guyville*, sang backup on *The Honeymoon Suite* (1993) and opened some of their early shows. The name came from a radio DJ mispronouncing "Astro Boy" during an interview and Lee deciding to keep it. By late 1993 they were playing Lounge Ax and the Empty Bottle regularly — two rooms that between them defined what Chicago indie looked like from the floor.

1995.blurb: By 1995, Ashtray Boy was operating as two bands simultaneously — one in Chicago, one in Sydney — with Randall Lee moving between them. *Candypants Beach* (1995) and *The Everyman's Fourth Dimension* (1996) drew on material from both rosters. In Chicago the shows ran toward the intimate: the Empty Bottle three times across 1995 and 1996, a boat cruise on the Chicago River in September 1997, a university hall on the South Side, a final return to Lounge Ax in October. The geography made conventional touring difficult, so the band built its American audience one Chicago room at a time.

1999.blurb: Lounge Ax — the Lincoln Avenue room that had been home to Ashtray Boy since their first Chicago show in 1992 — closed in January 2000. The December 22, 1999 show there was one of the last. The following month, the band was at the Empty Bottle. The transition between those two dates captures something about what happened to the Chicago scene at the turn of the decade: the rooms that had defined it in the early nineties were closing, and the audience was redistributing to the venues that remained. *There's Your Heart* (1999) and *The King's Buccaneer* (2000) arrived in this moment of reorganization.

2002.blurb: The December 22, 2002 show at the Empty Bottle — two years after *The King's Buccaneer* and two years before *The Euro* — documents the band in a quiet interlude. Randall Lee was still moving between Australia and the United States, still anchoring the Chicago end of the operation at the Empty Bottle, which by this point had absorbed much of the audience that once filled Lounge Ax. No album was pending, no tour in progress; the show is evidence of a band that maintained a presence in its adopted city regardless of release cycles.

2007.blurb: The July 17, 2007 show at Schubas Tavern on Belmont is the lone documented Chicago appearance in what became a six-year gap between studio albums. By 2007 Schubas — with its attached Harmony Grill and 150-person capacity — had become one of the city's reliable rooms for established indie acts with modest but loyal audiences. The move from the Empty Bottle to Schubas marks a subtle shift in the band's Chicago trajectory: still present, still drawing, but at a slightly different altitude than the formative years on Lounge Ax.

2011.blurb: *Together* (2013) was the ninth Ashtray Boy record, arriving two decades into the project and with the band now nominally Melbourne-based. The Chicago shows that bracket this release — two in the fall of 2011 and one in December 2013 at the Hideout — mark the end of an era for the band's American presence. The Hideout, with its bar-in-a-house architecture on Wabansia, was by this point one of the last venues still serving the audience that had come of age at Lounge Ax. That Ashtray Boy played there at the close of the *Together* cycle feels like a full loop.

2016.blurb: *Painted with the Mouth* (2015) — Ashtray Boy's tenth album — brought Randall Lee back to Chicago for the February 28, 2016 show at Township on Milwaukee Avenue. By this point the band was Melbourne-based, the Chicago operation reduced to occasional visits from the city that had incubated them in the early nineties. Township — part bar, part gallery, part music venue — is a different room from the Lounge Ax and Empty Bottle where this history began; the audience for that era has aged into it. The arc from a Lounge Ax debut in July 1992 to a Township show in February 2016 covers the full geography of a Chicago indie institution that was never quite a Chicago band.

1988.blurb: David Grubbs had come north from Louisville and Squirrel Bait, settling in Chicago where Bastro formed around him with Bundy K. Brown on bass and eventually John McEntire on drums. Four albums on Homestead and Touch and Go across four years, all of it played at full volume. The archive catches them across three Chicago rooms in four years: Cubby Bear on Clark, the Czar Bar on Sheffield, Lounge Ax on Lincoln — the Chicago circuit for a band too abrasive for mainstream college radio but too disciplined for the noise underground. Grubbs left a University of Chicago PhD program to tour Europe in 1991; the chair of the English department told him it wouldn't work. By the end of 1991 Bastro had become Gastr del Sol, and McEntire was moving toward what would become Tortoise.

quotes.text: With Bastro it only sounded best at full volume, so we were always hostage to terrible live sound.
The chair of the English department basically said 'this won't work. You can't be an academic and a touring musician.' One of the better decisions of my life was to not listen to him.

2004.blurb: Sebadoh went quiet after *The Sebadoh* (1999), Lou Barlow absorbed into Folk Implosion and solo work while Jason Loewenstein and Eric Gaffney pursued their own projects. The 2004 reunion came without a new album — Barlow described it as the "Turbo Acoustic" tour, a stripped-down return to the circuit before any commitment to recording. The April 20 show at the Abbey Pub on Chicago's northwest side documents this moment: a band testing whether the audience and the chemistry still existed, not yet knowing that the Dinosaur Jr. reunion in 2005 would pull Barlow away again for several years. The Abbey Pub was the right room for this kind of provisional return — honest-sized, no pretense.

2011.blurb: *Defend Yourself* (2013) was Sebadoh's first studio album in fourteen years, made with a new drummer — Bob D'Amico replacing Eric Gaffney — and written by Barlow through the end of a marriage and the beginning of a new relationship, with children now in the picture. Schubas Tavern in Chicago's Lakeview neighborhood: four shows across four years, 2011 through 2015. The 150-cap room with its wooden bar and Christmas lights represents a precise calibration of where Sebadoh sat in the early 2010s — the kind of band that fills Schubas every time it comes through because the audience that found them in 1993 or 1994 still shows up, and still fits in the room.

quotes.text: We still battle it out from record to record and try to make ends meet, but now it's even more necessary to make sure that everything is cost effective.
quotes.attr: Lou Barlow, *The Line of Best Fit*, October 2013

quotes.text: Touring was really good, and I think that's when we really started to definitively think about doing a new record.
quotes.attr: Lou Barlow, *The Line of Best Fit*, October 2013

1985.blurb: Between 1985 and 1988, Sonic Youth released four albums on three different independent labels — Homestead, SST, Enigma — and toured constantly, running a circuit that took them through Chicago's Cabaret Metro three times in four years. Kim Gordon was still working day jobs into the mid-1980s; the band was making noise-art records with out-of-tune guitars that didn't have obvious commercial prospects. *Daydream Nation* (1988) changed the calculation. By November of that year, when they played the Metro on the *Daydream Nation* tour, DGC was already circling. The SST and Homestead years were ending.

quotes.text: I don't remember when I stopped having some kind of day job, but by the time we got to Daydream Nation [1988] I felt we were really on it.
quotes.attr: Kim Gordon, *Girl in a Band* (memoir, Harper Collins, 2015)

2002.blurb: *Murray Street* (2002) was named after the block in lower Manhattan closest to the World Trade Center site, where the band had their rehearsal studio. They had watched the towers fall from their neighborhood. The album was quieter and more introspective than much of their DGC catalog — Jim O'Rourke, the Chicago musician who had joined as a full member, pushed the production toward long instrumental passages and restraint. The August 17 Metro show was part of the North American leg of the *Murray Street* tour, the same circuit they'd run as independents in the 1980s, now on a major label budget but playing rooms not much bigger than where they'd started.

2006.blurb: *Rather Ripped* (2006) was the last album Sonic Youth made for DGC/Geffen before leaving the major label system for Matador. *The Eternal* (2009) was the first indie release in two decades, and the June 2009 show at the Vic Theatre on Sheffield — a 1,400-seat room with balconies and chandeliers — was part of that tour. The Vic was a step up from the Metro, which was itself a step up from the rooms they'd played in the 1980s. Twenty-five years of circuit-building had produced a band that could fill a theatre on Chicago's North Side on a Saturday night. The Eternal tour was also their last. Thurston Moore and Kim Gordon separated in 2011 and the band dissolved.

1993.blurb: Stereolab in October 1993 was a London band doing the American Midwest: Grand Rapids on a Thursday, a Reckless Records in-store in Chicago on Saturday, Minneapolis Friday and Saturday (two shows on the Saturday, 7th Street Entry and Northern Lights), before the tour wrapped back in London in December. Tim Gane and Lætitia Sadier had been together since 1988 and running Stereolab since 1990, working with Too Pure in the UK and licensing to Elektra for the US — the kind of arrangement that got you on the indie circuit without a major's overhead or its interference. They were motorik drones and French-accented vocals in rooms that had mostly heard American bands. The Midwest crowds had no obvious frame for them, and that was part of the point.

quotes.text: We get what we're given. We're too polite to demand anything although we always ask for cider.

1995.blurb: By 1995 Stereolab was filling Lounge Ax twice in a single night — early show and late show, July 31, the two performances documented separately in the archive. *Emperor Tomato Ketchup* had arrived that year, Elektra's biggest push for the band, and the American audience that found them strange in 1993 had expanded considerably. The move to the Metro for 1996 and then two nights there in November 1997 for *Dots and Loops* tracks the upgrade in scale: from 300-cap rooms to 1,100. They were also losing Andy Ramsay to a personal crisis during the *Dots* period — the band absorbing the loss quietly while continuing to release and tour with the kind of productivity that defined their entire run.

2004.blurb: Tim Gane and Lætitia Sadier had ended their personal relationship by the time *Margerine Eclipse* arrived in 2004, the album written partly in the aftermath of the death of founding member Mary Hansen in a cycling accident in 2002. The band continued — two Vic Theatre shows in Chicago, April 2004 and March 2006 — but the ensemble had changed shape, the personnel more fluid, the creative center shifted. The Vic, at 1,400 capacity, was the largest room on their Chicago circuit, a venue they'd graduated to after a decade moving from Reckless Records in-stores to Lounge Ax to the Metro. The 2006 show for *Fab Four Suture* was among their last American dates before an extended pause that preceded the band's eventual dissolution in 2009.

The Vic, at 1,400 capacity, was the largest room on their Chicago circuit, a venue they'd graduated to after a decade moving from Reckless Records in-stores to Lounge Ax to the Metro. The 2006 show for *Fab Four Suture* was among their last American dates before an extended pause that preceded the band's eventual dissolution in 2009.

1987.blurb: Martin Phillipps had been running The Chills out of Dunedin, New Zealand since the early 1980s, cycling through enough band members to field a cricket team, keeping the name and the sensibility constant through the turnover. *Brave Words* (1987) was the UK release that gave them a toehold in Britain, where the NME and Melody Maker had been paying attention to Flying Nun for years. The December 1987 show at the Town & Country in Leeds — a 2,000-capacity venue — was a long way from the Dunedin practice rooms where the band had developed. The gap between Flying Nun's reach and the rooms they could now access in the UK was, briefly, an extraordinary thing.

1990.blurb: *Submarine Bells* (1990) was The Chills' American major label debut on Slash/Reprise, and the spring 1990 US tour was their attempt to make the jump: Chapel Hill to Boston to Chicago (Reckless Records in-store followed the same day by Shank Hall in Milwaukee) to Minneapolis (in-store at Oar Folkjokeopus, then 7th Street Entry that same evening) to St. Louis. Two in-stores and six proper shows in two weeks, the Midwest indie circuit run in sequence. By 1992 and *Soft Bomb*, the major label ambitions had dimmed; the band was back to Lounge Ax for two nights in September. Phillipps later described the period as "feeling its passing as we disappeared into the bowels of the Warners machine."

quotes.text: A paean to the early 'Dunedin Sound' and feeling its passing as we disappeared into the bowels of the Warners machine.

2019.blurb: The Chills had been largely absent since the early 1990s collapse of the Slash/Reprise deal and the years of instability that followed, before *Silver Bullets* (2015) marked a genuine return and *Snowbound* (2018) confirmed it was sustained. The February 2019 show at the Empty Bottle in Chicago — a 250-cap room on Western Avenue — was part of a North American run supporting *Snowbound*. The Empty Bottle in 2019 was the logical room: it accommodated the audience that still cared, which is a loyal but finite group, and it didn't ask the band to pretend they were something they weren't. Martin Phillipps had been running this project for nearly four decades at this point; the Empty Bottle show documents him still at it.

1988.blurb: The Feelies spent 1988 navigating the tension between their growing fame and a deep-seated aversion to life on the road. While supporting their major-label debut, Only Life, they prioritized the intimate energy of small clubs over the professional demands of larger theaters. This year was defined by high-profile opening slots that often reinforced their preference for the creative comfort of their home base in Haledon.

quotes.text: Touring is OK, but we just hate being away from home for too long.
We liked the jam-packed clubs. We saw a lot of value in staying where we were at.
It’s not fun, it’s comical. You are told not to talk to him, not to look him in the eye. [Regarding opening for Bob Dylan]

2008.blurb: New Jersey art-rock band reunited in 2008 after a 17-year hiatus, known for frenetic live performances and meticulous studio work.

quotes.text: We were getting kind of burnt with playing and touring at that point.

2005.blurb: David Gedge had spent much of 1998–2004 running Cinerama, his cinematic side project with Sally Murrell, before reconstituting The Wedding Present for touring in 2004–2005. The band that came back was built around Gedge and a rotating cast of musicians — the lineup had always been fluid after the original Leeds core dispersed — and the shows in 2005 and 2006 preceded the first new Wedding Present studio album in over a decade. Gedge's approach to anniversary touring (the band would periodically perform entire albums start to finish) had built a loyal audience that followed the project regardless of what Gedge called it; the rooms were smaller than the Bizarre Festival days but the attendance was reliable.

2010.blurb: *Valentina* (2012) was the first new Wedding Present studio album in sixteen years, arriving on Gedge's own Scopitones label and made possible by a PledgeMusic campaign — the band funding the record through its audience before a label existed to release it. The 2010 KEXP session in Seattle and the March 2012 Double Door show in Chicago bracket the making and release: the KEXP performance comes in the buildup, the Double Door show on the *Valentina* tour. Double Door in Chicago's Wicker Park, at about 500 capacity, was the room that fit the band's American draw in 2012 — enough people to make the show feel full, not so many that the economics required a booking agent who'd also work arena acts.

2017.blurb: *Going, Going...* (2016) arrived thirty years into David Gedge's run with The Wedding Present, and the 2017–2018 touring cycle ran through the anniversary circuit alongside it. By this period the band had also begun the practice of performing their landmark albums in full — *Seamonsters* in particular got regular anniversary treatment — which gave the touring a dual track: promoting new material for an audience that had never stopped showing up, while replaying the catalog for audiences who came specifically for the older records. Gedge had kept the band on the road with minimal interruption across three decades; the touring structure was the institution, and the albums were the occasions for it.

1993.blurb: Versus formed in New York in 1990 around guitarist Richard Baluyut and bassist Fontaine Toups, whose interlocking male/female harmonies and angular guitar interplay — indebted to Mission of Burma more than to whatever was selling that year — gave them a sound that found its audience through touring rather than radio. *Let's Electrify* (1993) on Remora and *The Stars Are Insane* (1994) on TeenBeat marked their first two years on record. In Chicago they played Lounge Ax three times in an eighteen-month stretch, and in September 1994 moved across town to the Double Door in Wicker Park — a room with twice the capacity, which tells you something about where they were headed.

quotes.text: I missed the minutiae of touring (like driving around in a van) as much as playing to audiences.

1996.blurb: Signing to Caroline Records for *Secret Swingers* (1996) meant access to wider distribution and a booking agent who could get them onto the Lollapalooza second stage in August 1995 alongside Beck and Hum. The Chicago shows tell the story of the upgrade: Lounge Ax in May 1996, then in November a Reckless Records in-store followed the same evening by the Metro — a 1,100-capacity room on Clark Street that represented a genuine jump from the 300-cap rooms of the early years. They played the Metro again in April 1997 and May 1998 for *Two Cents Plus Tax*, Caroline's attempt at something bigger. One year in this stretch they logged 120 shows including two European runs.

quotes.text: One year we did 120 shows, including two jaunts to Europe, so it got to be too much for him [Edward].

2000.blurb: *Hurrah* (Merge, 2000) arrived after Caroline dropped them, and the band's Chicago presence had shifted accordingly — Lounge Ax was now closed, the Metro was behind them, and the Empty Bottle became the room. Two shows there in 2000: May and October, bookending the album cycle. The band also opened for Sleater-Kinney on *The Hot Rock* tour that year. By 2001 they had broken up, the core members relocating to San Francisco and redirecting into side projects. The two Empty Bottle shows document the tail end of a ten-year run — not a dramatic close, just a band quietly finishing what it had started.

2003.blurb: After the band nominally dissolved in 2001, Richard Baluyut and Fontaine Toups were still occasionally performing together — two shows at the Abbey Pub on Chicago's northwest side, January 2003 and April 2004, appear in the archive from this period. The Abbey Pub at Elston and Addison was a beer-and-pinball room with a back stage that hosted the surviving audience from the Lounge Ax era without pretending to be anything larger. The full reunion wouldn't be announced until 2007. These shows are what the gap looked like from the floor: quiet, unannounced, a band that hadn't quite stopped.

2002.blurb: Wire had been dormant since 1991 when they reconvened in 2000, releasing the *Read & Burn* EPs across 2002 as both a creative restart and a statement about format — short, punishing records that didn't ask for your patience. *Send* (2003) extended the approach into a full album. The November 2002 Melkweg show in Amsterdam, recorded at the Crossing Border festival, documents the band in the early phase of the reunion: still finding the shape of what a 2002 Wire performance looked like as distinct from what the original band had done in 1977. Colin Newman and Graham Lewis were in their forties. They had invented post-punk the first time around and now had to figure out what came after reinventing it.

2013.blurb: Three albums in five years — *Change Becomes Us* (2013), the self-titled *Wire* (2015), *Silver/Lead* (2017) — marked the most sustained creative run the band had managed since the original trio of *Pink Flag*, *Chairs Missing*, and *154* in the late 1970s. *Change Becomes Us* was built from songs the band had written but never recorded in the early 1980s, a confrontation with unfinished business that came off less as nostalgia than as archaeology. The touring across this period followed the releases rather than chasing growth: rooms that fit the audience they had, in the cities where that audience reliably showed up, with a precision that had always been part of how Wire operated.

2020.blurb: *10:20* (2020) arrived as touring became impossible — the album's release coinciding almost exactly with the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns. Wire had planned a supporting tour; it didn't happen. The record is an unusual document as a result: a band that had been releasing and touring with consistent discipline since reforming in 2000 suddenly without a road component, the album existing in the world without the live performances that typically anchor it in memory. For a band whose reputation was built in part on the precision and economy of their live shows, the absence is not incidental.
